paragraphs: The gentleman of leisure in the quasi-peaceable stage, then, not only consumes more of the staff of life than he needs for subsistence and physical efficiency. His consumption also becomes specialised with regard to the quality of the goods. He consumes freely and of the best, in food, drink, narcotics, shelter, services, ornaments, clothing, weapons and equipment, amusements, amulets, and idols or divinities. These articles gradually improve over time, and the main motive behind each innovation is no doubt the greater efficiency of the improved, more elaborate products for personal comfort and well-being. Yet this does not remain the only purpose of their consumption. The canon of reputability is close at hand, and it seizes upon those innovations which, by its standard, are fit to survive. Since consuming these superior goods is evidence of wealth, it becomes honorific. Conversely, failing to consume in due quantity and quality becomes a mark of inferiority and demerit.

This growing, careful discrimination about quality in eating, drinking and so on soon affects not only the gentleman's manner of life but also his training and intellectual activity. He is no longer merely the successful, aggressive male, the man of strength, resource and courage. To avoid appearing dull, he must cultivate his tastes, since it is now his duty to distinguish with some precision between the noble and the ignoble in consumable goods. He becomes a connoisseur of food of various degrees of merit, of manly drinks and trinkets, of suitable clothing and architecture, of weapons, games, dancers and narcotics. This cultivation of aesthetic judgement demands time and application. Consequently, his life of leisure tends to turn into a fairly arduous effort to learn how to live a life of ostensible leisure in a becoming way. Closely related to the requirement that he consume freely and choose the right goods is a second requirement: he must know how to consume them in a seemly manner. His leisure must be conducted in due form. From this, good manners arise, as an earlier chapter showed. High-bred manners and ways of living are forms of conformity to the norm of conspicuous leisure and conspicuous consumption.

Conspicuous consumption of valuable goods is a means of gaining reputability for the gentleman of leisure. However, as wealth accumulates in his hands, his own unaided effort is no longer enough to display his opulence in this way. He therefore calls on the help of friends and competitors by giving valuable presents and expensive feasts and entertainments. Presents and feasts probably had an origin other than naive ostentation. Still, they acquired this usefulness very early and have kept it to the present, so that it has long been the real ground on which these customs rest. Costly entertainments, such as the potlatch or the ball, are particularly suited to this end. Through them, the competitor with whom the host wishes to compare himself is made to serve as a means to that end. He consumes vicariously for his host. At the same time, he witnesses the excess of good things that the host cannot dispose of single-handed, and he observes the host's ease in matters of etiquette.
